query: For noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials used in catalysis, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs reliable material formation and the resulting catalytic performance, and why? Specify one controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The formation of single-phase noble metal-based high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles is governed by the reduction of all individual elements, which favors the crystallization of HEA nanoparticles with a uniform chemical composition and homogeneous size distribution.
generation.intervention: Combining multiple elements in the precursor mixture
generation.conditions: Heating under continuous stirring, followed by cooling and crystallization
generation.structural_mediator: Crystallization of a metallic phase with a defect-rich and small domain size
generation.mechanism: Reduction of individual elements, followed by crystallization of a single-phase HEA nanoparticle
generation.predicted_outcome: Uniform chemical composition and homogeneous size distribution of HEA nanoparticles
generation.boundary: Within the range of 5 to 35 at% of each metal element in the HEA
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of crystallization and the role of defects in the HEA structure

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of HEA nanoparticles synthesized with multimetallic and bimetallic precursor mixtures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles synthesized with multimetallic precursor mixtures do not exhibit a uniform chemical composition and homogeneous size distribution, the hypothesis is falsified.

## Material synthesis
All samples were prepared following a literature procedure described by Yusenko et al. All compounds were prepared from commercial metal precursors (Sigma Aldrich). As cationic precursors the chloropentaammine metal chlorides of Ir, Rh, and Ru were used; Ir(NH3)5Cl]Cl2, [Rh(NH3)5Cl]Cl2, and [Ru(NH3)5Cl]Cl2. The anionic precursors were the ammonium hexachlorometallates of Ir, Pt, and Os; (NH4)2[IrCl6], (NH4)2[PtCl6], and (NH4)2[OsCl6]. In short, separate aqueous solutions of anionic metal precursors (hexachlorates) and cationic metal precursors (chloropentaamines) were prepared by dissolving the respective amounts of the individual metal salts in hot MilliQ water (90 °C). To obtain a qualitative measure of the mixing enthalpies of the bimetallic and HEA systems in both fcc and hcp crystal structures, the total energy of several bulk structures was calculated with density functional theory. The calculations used the revised Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (RPBE) exchange–correlation functional as implemented in the GPAW code. Each system was calculated as both fcc and hcp structures containing 32 and 16 atoms per cell, respectively. The elements of each atom in the binary systems were chosen randomly with equal probability and the elements in the HEA systems were chosen with probabilities corresponding to the precursor compositions: Ru0.11Rh0.26Os0.06Ir0.22Pt0.35 for the fcc-structure and Ru0.31Rh0.09Os0.30Ir0.15Pt0.15 for the hcp-structure. In all cases, the cell was scaled to the weighted mean of the lattice constants of the atoms constituting the cell. In principle, HEAs are produced by alloying five or more metal elements in nearly equal proportions (recently extended to 5 to 35 at%) into solid solutions with a high mixing entropy rather than an intermetallic phase. The resulting synergistic effect endows HEAs with high mechanical strength, good thermal stability, and catalytic activity. In particularly, HEAs displayed appraisable catalytic performance in electrocatalytic water splitting, ammonia oxidation and decomposition, and CO2 reduction. Mechanistic studies suggest that the ligand effect and distortion effect of HEAs, which arise from tuning the composition and geometric properties of HEAs to a large degree, could significantly modify the electronic properties of active sites and consequently improve their catalytic performance. The inherent synergy effect of HEAs provides possibility to boost the catalytic activity by combining suitable metals.
